The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC and let $G\sim N(0,\sigma^2)$ for $\sigma\ge0$. Then $\mathbb E[G^2]=\sigma^2$ and $\mathbb E[G^4]=3\sigma^4$; in particular the fourth moment is finite. For independent centered normal coordinates $G_j\sim N(0,\sigma_j^2)$, every finite linear combination of the variables $G_j^2$ has finite second moment.
Assume AC. If a centered row-wise independent triangular array has finite second moments, $s_n>0$ and the Lindeberg condition, then $$s_n^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^{k_n}X_{n,k}\Rightarrow N(0,1).$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim: By [F1], each $V_{n,j}=G_{n,j}^2-1$ is centered with variance $2$. Independence within each row gives $\mathbb E T_n=0$ and $\operatorname{Var}(T_n)=2\sum_jw_{n,j}^2=1$. Thus the row standard deviation is $s_n=1>0$.

Fix $\delta>0$ and put $w_n^* =\max_jw_{n,j}$. If $w_{n,j}=0$, its Lindeberg summand is zero. Otherwise $w_{n,j}|V_{n,j}|>\delta$ implies $|V_{n,j}|>\delta/w_n^*$. This is the Lindeberg condition for the array $w_{n,j}V_{n,j}$.
The array in step 2.1 is centered and independent within rows, has finite second moments, and has row standard deviation $1$. By [F2] and the Lindeberg condition just proved, $T_n\Rightarrow N(0,1)$.

Let $a=(a_j)$ be a positive nondecreasing sequence with $a_j\to\infty$, and let $\sigma=(\sigma_j)$ be a positive nondecreasing sequence with $\sigma_j\to\infty$. For $\varepsilon>0$, put $\eta_j=\theta_j/\sigma_j$ and observe $Y_j=Z_j/\sigma_j=\eta_j+\varepsilon\xi_j$, where $Z$ is the normalized observation in the Gaussian sequence inverse model and the $\xi_j$ are independent standard normal random variables. For $0<q\le2$ and $r>0$, define
$$\Theta_q(r)=\left\{\eta\in\mathbb R^{\mathbb N_{>0}}:(\sigma_j\eta_j)_{j\ge1}\in\ell^2,\ \sum_{j=1}^{\infty}|a_j\sigma_j\eta_j|^q\le1,\ \sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\sigma_j^2\eta_j^2\ge r^2\right\}.$$

$$\alpha_\varepsilon(\psi)=\mathbb E_{\varepsilon,0}\psi,\qquad \beta_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r),\psi)=\sup_{\eta\in\Theta_q(r)}\mathbb E_{\varepsilon,\eta}(1-\psi).$$
When $\Theta_q(r)=\varnothing$, define $\beta_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r),\psi)=\beta_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r),\alpha)=\gamma_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r))=0$, the convention that no type-II error occurs when no alternative is possible. For $\alpha\in(0,1)$ define
$$\beta_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r),\alpha)=\inf_{\psi:\,\alpha_\varepsilon(\psi)\le\alpha}\beta_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r),\psi),\qquad \gamma_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r))=\inf_\psi\{\alpha_\varepsilon(\psi)+\beta_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r),\psi)\}.$$

derivations.claim: Put $b_j=a_j^2$ and $c_j=\sigma_j^4$. For $0<A<b_1^{-1}$ define the finite sums $$N(A)=\sum_{j\ge1}c_j(1-Ab_j)_+,\qquad D(A)=\sum_{j\ge1}c_jb_j(1-Ab_j)_+,$$ and $R(A)=N(A)/D(A)$. The active set is finite because $b_j\to\infty$, and it is nonempty because $A<b_1^{-1}$. On every compact subinterval of $(0,b_1^{-1})$, only finitely many indices can be active; each summand is continuous and vanishes at its activation endpoint. Thus $R$ is continuous and $D(A)>0$.

The ratio is a weighted average of $1/b_j$: with $p_j(A)=c_jb_j(1-Ab_j)_+/D(A)$, the numbers $p_j(A)$ are nonnegative, sum to one, and $R(A)=\sum_jp_j(A)/b_j$. Fix $K>0$ and choose $j_0$ so $b_j\ge K$ for $j\ge j_0$. The head weight $\sum_{j<j_0}p_j(A)$ tends to zero as $A\downarrow0$: its numerator is bounded by the fixed finite sum $\sum_{j<j_0}c_jb_j$, while for any $M\ge j_0$ the denominator is at least $\frac12\sum_{j=j_0}^M c_jb_j$ once $A b_M\le1/2$. Since $c_jb_j\to\infty$, these finite partial sums can be made arbitrarily large. Also $R(A)\le b_1^{-1}\sum_{j<j_0}p_j(A)+1/K$, so $\limsup_{A\downarrow0}R(A)\le1/K$. As $K$ is arbitrary, $R(A)\to0$.

Let $m_0$ be the largest index with $b_{m_0}=b_1$; it is finite because $b_j\to\infty$. For $A$ sufficiently close to $b_1^{-1}$ from below, the active set is exactly $\{1,\ldots,m_0\}$ and all its $b_j$ equal $b_1$. Hence $R(A)=b_1^{-1}$ there.

By step 1.1, $R$ is continuous on $(0,b_1^{-1})$. Given $r^2\in(0,b_1^{-1})$, steps 2.1 and 2.2 let us choose $0<A_-<A_+<b_1^{-1}$ with $R(A_-)<r^2$ and $R(A_+)=b_1^{-1}$. Apply [F2] to the restriction of $R$ to $[A_-,A_+]$ to obtain $A$ with $R(A)=r^2$. Set $z_0^2=r^2/N(A)>0$ and define $\widetilde\eta_j^2=z_0^2\sigma_j^2(1-Ab_j)_+$. Its support is the finite active set, and $$\sum_j\sigma_j^2\widetilde\eta_j^2=z_0^2N(A)=r^2,\qquad \sum_ja_j^2\sigma_j^2\widetilde\eta_j^2=z_0^2D(A)=\frac{r^2D(A)}{N(A)}=1.$$ Taking $r_0=b_1^{-1/2}$ proves the assertion and, by [F1], the profile belongs to $\Theta_2(r)$.

Fix any $\eta\in\Theta_2(r)$ and put $x_j=\eta_j^2$ and $\widetilde x_j=\widetilde\eta_j^2$. Both series $\sum_j\sigma_j^2x_j$ and $\sum_ja_j^2\sigma_j^2x_j$ are finite by [F1], so their displayed difference is absolutely convergent. Multiplying the inequality by $z_0^2$ therefore gives $\sum_j\widetilde x_jx_j\ge\sum_j\widetilde x_j^2$.

Expanding the difference of squared $\ell^2$ norms of the nonnegative sequences $x$ and $\widetilde x$ gives $$\sum_j\eta_j^4-\sum_j\widetilde\eta_j^4=\sum_j(x_j-\widetilde x_j)^2+2\sum_j\widetilde x_j(x_j-\widetilde x_j)\ge0$$ by step 1.2. The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $X$ and $Y$ be real Hilbert spaces and let $K:X\to Y$ be a compact linear operator of infinite rank, viewed as an inverse model with exact datum $Kx$. Here compact means that the image of every bounded subset has compact closure. Write $N(K)=\{x\in X:Kx=0\}$ and $H_0=\overline{\operatorname{ran}K}$. Fix a positive singular system $(s_j,v_j,u_j)_{j\in\mathbb N_{>0}}$ for $K$, where $\mathbb N_{>0}=\{1,2,3,\ldots\}$, $s_1\ge s_2\ge\cdots>0$, $s_j\to0$, $Kv_j=s_ju_j$, $(v_j)$ is a complete orthonormal basis of $N(K)^\perp$, and $(u_j)$ is a complete orthonormal basis of $H_0$. A complete orthonormal basis is an orthonormal family whose closed linear span is the whole indicated subspace. These are the compact SVD conventions; in particular, this model concerns minimum-norm representatives in $N(K)^\perp$ and does not estimate a kernel component.

For a truth $x\in N(K)^\perp$, let $\theta_j=\langle x,v_j\rangle_X$. The complete-basis coefficient map identifies $N(K)^\perp$ bijectively and isometrically with $\ell^2(\mathbb N_{>0},\mathbb R)$, so every $\theta\in\ell^2(\mathbb N_{>0},\mathbb R)$ is a model parameter. For $\epsilon>0$, take the functional white-noise experiment on the separable Hilbert space $H_0$ with observations $Y_x(g)=\langle Kx,g\rangle_Y+\epsilon W(g)$, where $W$ is centered, has covariance $\mathbb E[W(g)W(h)]=\langle g,h\rangle_Y$, and has independent standard-normal values on every finite orthonormal tuple. The countable complete basis makes $H_0$ separable. Define $\xi_j=W(u_j)$ and $Z_j=Y_x(u_j)/s_j$. The sequence sample space is $\mathbb R^{\mathbb N_{>0}}$ with the product Borel sigma-algebra, meaning the sigma-algebra generated by its coordinate projections. The coordinate law is the pushforward of the functional experiment under $y\mapsto(y(u_j)/s_j)_{j\in\mathbb N_{>0}}$; this map is measurable because each coordinate is a cylinder evaluation followed by scalar multiplication. The compact SVD expansion gives $\langle Kx,u_j\rangle_Y=s_j\theta_j$, and the positive-noise white-noise coordinate theorem gives the independent standard-normal coordinates $\xi_j$. Hence the normalized coordinates satisfy $Z_j=\theta_j+\epsilon s_j^{-1}\xi_j,\qquad j\in\mathbb N_{>0}.$

For the zero-noise boundary $\epsilon=0$, define the sequence experiment separately by the point mass at $\theta$, so $Z_j=\theta_j$. This boundary is not an instance of the positive-noise functional experiment.

Let $H$ be a separable real Hilbert space with a fixed complete orthonormal basis $(u_j)$, indexed by $J=\{1,\ldots,m\}$ for $m\in\mathbb N_0$ or by $J=\mathbb N_{>0}$; the empty basis covers $H=\{0\}$. Let $Y_x(g)=\langle Kx,g\rangle_H+\epsilon Z(g)$ be the isonormal white-noise experiment with $\epsilon>0$, and write $\mu_j=\langle Kx,u_j\rangle_H$. For every parameter $x$ and every basis index $j$, the observations $Y_x(u_j)$ are independent and have laws $N(\mu_j,\epsilon^2)$, where $N$ is the scalar normal law defined in the experiment.

For $g\in H$, set $P_Ng=\sum_{j\in J,\ j\le N}\langle g,u_j\rangle_Hu_j$, with $P_N=I$ once all vectors of a finite basis have been included. Then

$$Y_x(g)=L^2(\mathbb P)\text{-}\lim_{N\to\infty}\sum_{j\in J,\ j\le N}\langle g,u_j\rangle_HY_x(u_j).$$

Thus every finite collection of observation functionals is reconstructed from the coefficient sequence in mean square. This does not assert almost-sure convergence of the full sequence of partial sums, a simultaneous path identity for all test vectors, or an $H$-valued observation.

More precisely, let $\mathcal C_H$ be the cylinder sigma-algebra on $\mathbb R^H$, let $\mathcal C_J$ be the sigma-algebra on $\mathbb R^J$ generated by its coordinate evaluations, and let $P_x$ be the field sampling law. Define $S:\mathbb R^H\to\mathbb R^J$ by $S(y)_j=y(u_j)$ and $Q_x=S_*P_x$, where a pushforward is $S_*P_x(B)=P_x(S^{-1}(B))$. There is a measurable map $T:(\mathbb R^J,\mathcal C_J)\to(\mathbb R^H,\mathcal C_H)$, depending only on the indexed basis, such that for every parameter $x$,

$$S_*P_x=Q_x,\qquad T_*Q_x=P_x,\qquad S\circ T=\operatorname{id}_{\mathbb R^J}.$$

These parameter-independent maps give equivalence of the field cylinder experiment and its coefficient experiment. One such map is the following. For $k\ge1$ and $g\in H$, let $N_k(g)$ be the least integer $N\ge k$ with $\|g-P_Ng\|_H\le2^{-k}$ and put

$$a_{g,k}(z)=\sum_{j\in J,\ j\le N_k(g)}\langle g,u_j\rangle_Hz_j,\qquad T(z)(g)=\begin{cases}\lim_{k\to\infty}a_{g,k}(z),&\text{if the limit exists in }\mathbb R,\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}$$

For each fixed $x$ and $g$, $T(S(Y_x))(g)=Y_x(g)$ almost surely, and the same holds jointly for each fixed finite list of test vectors. The exceptional event may depend on $x$ and on that list; no intersection over all $g\in H$ is asserted. In dimension zero the coefficient space is a singleton and $T$ returns the field with value zero at $g=0$.

If $H=L^2([0,1])$ and the basis is one of the wavelet or trigonometric bases used to define the negative Sobolev carrier $H(\delta)$, then under countable choice and for $\delta>1/2$ the same coordinate sequence is a Borel Gaussian random element in $H(\delta)$ with mean coefficients $Kx$ and noise level $\epsilon$. In infinite dimension it is not an $L^2([0,1])$-valued sample.

Assume Countable Choice and use the Gaussian sequence inverse model with singular values $s_j>0$, inverse-noise weights $\sigma_j=s_j^{-1}$, and parameter coordinates $\theta=(\theta_j)\in\ell^2$. Let $a=(a_j)$ be a positive nondecreasing sequence with $a_j\to\infty$, and let $\sigma=(\sigma_j)$ be a positive nondecreasing sequence with $\sigma_j\to\infty$. For $\varepsilon>0$, put $\eta_j=\theta_j/\sigma_j$ and observe $Y_j=Z_j/\sigma_j=\eta_j+\varepsilon\xi_j$, where $Z$ is the normalized observation in the Gaussian sequence inverse model and the $\xi_j$ are independent standard normal random variables. For $0<q\le2$ and $r>0$, define
$$\Theta_q(r)=\left\{\eta\in\mathbb R^{\mathbb N_{>0}}:(\sigma_j\eta_j)_{j\ge1}\in\ell^2,\ \sum_{j=1}^{\infty}|a_j\sigma_j\eta_j|^q\le1,\ \sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\sigma_j^2\eta_j^2\ge r^2\right\}.$$
Test $H_0:\eta=0$ against $H_1:\eta\in\Theta_q(r)$ by a product-Borel measurable randomized test $\psi:\mathbb R^{\mathbb N_{>0}}\to[0,1]$, where $\psi(y)$ is the rejection probability. Its type-I error and maximal type-II error are
$$\alpha_\varepsilon(\psi)=\mathbb E_{\varepsilon,0}\psi,\qquad \beta_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r),\psi)=\sup_{\eta\in\Theta_q(r)}\mathbb E_{\varepsilon,\eta}(1-\psi).$$
When $\Theta_q(r)=\varnothing$, define $\beta_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r),\psi)=\beta_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r),\alpha)=\gamma_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r))=0$, the convention that no type-II error occurs when no alternative is possible. For $\alpha\in(0,1)$ define
$$\beta_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r),\alpha)=\inf_{\psi:\,\alpha_\varepsilon(\psi)\le\alpha}\beta_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r),\psi),\qquad \gamma_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r))=\inf_\psi\{\alpha_\varepsilon(\psi)+\beta_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r),\psi)\}.$$
A positive family $r_\varepsilon^*\to0$ is a minimax separation rate if $\gamma_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r_\varepsilon))\to1$ and $\beta_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r_\varepsilon),\alpha)\to1-\alpha$ for every $\alpha\in(0,1)$ whenever $r_\varepsilon/r_\varepsilon^*\to0$, while $\gamma_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r_\varepsilon))\to0$ and $\beta_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r_\varepsilon),\alpha)\to0$ for every $\alpha\in(0,1)$ whenever $r_\varepsilon/r_\varepsilon^*\to\infty$.
Assume AC. The function $\phi(x)=e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}$ is positive and Borel measurable on $\mathbb R$, with Lebesgue integral one.

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$ and let $\mathcal A=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. If finite measures $\mu$ and $
u$ on $(X,\mathcal A)$ agree on $\mathcal P$ and satisfy $\mu(X)=
u(X)$, then $\mu=
u$ on $\mathcal A$.

The total-mass equality is separate because this library's pi-system convention does not require $X\in\mathcal P$.

Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
$(E,\mathcal E)$ (Probability measures and probability spaces). Their **total variation
distance** is

$$\lVert\mu-\nu\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal E}\bigl|\mu(A)-\nu(A)\bigr| .$$

For every event $A$ the difference $\mu(A)-\nu(A)$ is a real number in
$[-1,1]$, because both measures have total mass one; hence the set being
maximized is a nonempty subset of $[0,1]$ and the supremum lies in $[0,1]$.
The empty event and the whole space give the values $0$ and
$|\mu(E)-\nu(E)|=0$, so the distance is zero when $\mu=\nu$, and it is symmetric
in $\mu$ and $\nu$. This convention carries no factor $1/2$ in the supremum;
it is therefore not the total variation norm of the signed measure $\mu-\nu$,
which is twice the quantity above when that signed measure is considered on a
measurable space where the decomposition is attained. On a countable state
space with its power-set sigma-algebra the supremum equals the half-$\ell^1$
sum $\tfrac12\sum_{x\in E}|\mu(\{x\})-\nu(\{x\})|$; that identity is proved in
Half-$\ell^1$ formula for total variation on a countable space, not assumed here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice (The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

derivations.claim: For each sign vector $\tau\in\{-1,+1\}^J$, let $v^\tau_j=\tau_jv_j$ on $J$ and zero elsewhere. Absolute values and squares are unchanged, so every $v^\tau$ belongs to $\Theta_q(r)$.

Under the null, $X_j=Y_j/\varepsilon$ has density $\varphi$. For a fixed sign and coordinate, the density ratio for mean $\tau_jv_j$ versus zero is $\exp(\tau_jv_jY_j/\varepsilon^2-v_j^2/(2\varepsilon^2))$; completing the square using [F7] shows its null expectation is one.

Independence [F4] multiplies the one-coordinate ratios from step 1.2, giving the density ratio for the finite coordinate vector on each cylinder event. Its null expectation is the product of unit expectations, so it defines a probability measure on the full product space.

Cylinder events form a generating pi-system. The fixed-sign sampling law and the probability measure from step 2.1 agree on every cylinder, so [F5] gives equality on the product sigma-algebra and validates the full likelihood-ratio identity.

Averaging the fixed-sign likelihood ratios in step 3.1 over the finite sign set factors coordinatewise and gives $L_v=\prod_{j\in J}e^{-\delta_j/2}\cosh(\sqrt{\delta_j}X_j)$, where $\delta_j=v_j^2/\varepsilon^2$. This density is positive and has null expectation one.

For a standard normal $G$, [F7] and $\cosh^2t=(1+\cosh(2t))/2$ give $e^{-\delta}\mathbb E\cosh^2(\sqrt\delta G)=e^{-\delta}(1+e^{2\delta})/2=\cosh\delta$. Independence [F4] and step 4.1 therefore give $\mathbb E_0L_v^2=\prod_{j\in J}\cosh\delta_j$.

The function $g(t)=t^2/2-\log\cosh t$ is even, has $g(0)=0$, and for $t\ge0$ has derivative $g'(t)=t-\tanh t\ge0$, since $(\tanh t)'\le1$ and $\tanh0=0$. Thus $\cosh t\le e^{t^2/2}$ for all real $t$. Since $\sum_j\delta_j^2=2u(v)^2$, step 5.1 yields $\mathbb E_0(L_v-1)^2=\prod_j\cosh\delta_j-1\le e^{\frac12\sum_j\delta_j^2}-1=e^{u(v)^2}-1$.

Since $\mathbb E_0(L_v-1)=0$, the positive and negative parts of $L_v-1$ have equal integrals; hence every event $E$ satisfies $|P_{\pi_v}(E)-P_0(E)|\le\frac12\mathbb E_0|L_v-1|\le\frac12\sqrt{\mathbb E_0(L_v-1)^2}$. Approximate a randomized test $\psi$ by $N^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^N\mathbf1_{\{\psi\ge k/N\}}$; the event bound [F6] and uniform approximation error $N^{-1}$ give $|\mathbb E_{\pi_v}\psi-\mathbb E_0\psi|\le\|P_{\pi_v}-P_0\|_{\rm TV}$.

The maximal type-II error is at least its mixture average because every sign alternative lies in $\Theta_q(r)$. Therefore every test has total error at least $1-\|P_{\pi_v}-P_0\|_{\rm TV}$, and any level-$\alpha$ test has maximal type-II error at least $1-\alpha-\|P_{\pi_v}-P_0\|_{\rm TV}$. Taking the respective infima, then applying steps 6.1 and 7.1, proves both stated risk bounds.

derivations.claim: The finite coordinate density of $X_i$ with mean $\mu_i$ divided by its null density is $\exp(\mu_iX_i-\mu_i^2/2)$. Thus a finite uniform mixture of the two signs at a coordinate of absolute mean $z$ has likelihood $e^{-z^2/2}\cosh(zX_i)$, and the prior with probabilities $1-g,g/2,g/2$ at $0,z,-z$ has likelihood $1+g\xi_z(X_i)$, where $\xi_z(t)=e^{-z^2/2}\cosh(zt)-1$. Multiplication over finitely many coordinates is justified by [F7]. Off these coordinates the law is unchanged; equality first on finite cylinders and then [F9] proves the likelihood identity on the whole sequence sample space. Every prior below has finite coordinate support; no new countable product probability law is constructed.

Completing the square and applying [F5] to the given unit density gives $\mathbb E e^{tG}=e^{t^2/2}$. Consequently, by expanding the hyperbolic functions, $$\mathbb E\xi_z(G+\mu)=\cosh(z\mu)-1,\qquad \operatorname{Var}\xi_z(G+\mu)=\cosh(z^2)-1+(e^{z^2}-1)\sinh^2(z\mu).$$ For fixed $B$, $\mathbb E\xi_z(G)^4\le C_B(\cosh(z^2)-1)^2$ when $0<z\le B$: the bound $|\xi_z(G)|\le C_Bz^2(1+G^2)e^{B|G|}$ follows from the Taylor bound for $\cosh$ and $e^{-z^2/2}$, its fourth-power integral is finite by completing the square, and $\cosh(z^2)-1\ge z^4/2$. We will also use $\mathbb P(|G|>t)\le2e^{-t^2/2}$, obtained from [F6] and the same exponential moment, and the elementary Mills bounds $\overline\Phi(t)\le\phi(t)/t$ and $\overline\Phi(t)\ge\phi(t+1/t)/t$ for $t\ge1$. The first follows by integrating $x\phi(x)/t$ over $[t,\infty)$, and the second by integrating $\phi$ over $[t,t+1/t]$.

First suppose $\lambda>0$ and set $L=qs-2\beta>0$, $\kappa=L/(2-q)$. Use [F2] to define the unique positive $n,h_0$ by $$c_1h_0n^{2\beta+1}=r^2\varepsilon^{-2},\qquad c_2h_0n^{qs+1}=\varepsilon^{-q},\qquad U^2=c_0h_0^2n,$$ and put $z_i=z(i/n)$, $h_i=h_0d(i/n)$. Then $n^L=(c_1/c_2)\varepsilon^{2-q}/r^2$. The scalar certificate in [F2] gives $$\sum_{i\le m}h_i(\cosh(z_iv_i)-1)\ge\frac{h_0}2\left(n^{-2\beta}\sum_{i\le m}i^{2\beta}v_i^2-n^{-qs}\sum_{i\le m}i^{qs}|v_i|^q\right).$$ Also $\sum h_i<\infty$ and $V:=\sum h_i^2(\cosh(z_i^2)-1)\sim U^2$ as $n\to\infty$. These are score coefficients, which need not be at most one. On compact subsets of $0<r/r_\varepsilon^*<\infty$, $U$ stays bounded and bounded away from zero, $n$ grows as a positive power of $\varepsilon^{-1}$, and $h_0\asymp n^{-1/2}$.

In the Gaussian branch, with the profile notation of step 1.3, the extremal value in the Statement is exactly $J_\varepsilon(\widetilde r)$ in [F2], because $\cosh(z^2)-1=2\sinh^2(z^2/2)$. That lemma proves its power equivalent whenever $\widetilde r=o(\varepsilon^{a_c})$, equivalently when its associated $n\to\infty,h_0\to0$. Since $\widetilde r/r\to1$, this is the asserted restriction and the equivalent may be written with $r$. In particular on each compact transition range, $$u_\varepsilon\sim U=c_{\alpha,\beta,q}\varepsilon^{-A/D}r^{B/D}.$$ No equivalent outside the stated sufficient zone is used.

In the Gaussian branch, with the profile notation of step 1.3, for the Gaussian lower bound, fix a compact transition range. The feasible construction in [F2] can be made with expected energy $(1+\tau)r^2\varepsilon^{-2}$ and expected budget $(1-\tau)\varepsilon^{-q}$, on a finite window $a\le i/n'\le b$, with probabilities $g_i=h'_0d(i/n')\le1$ and amplitudes $z(i/n')$. Let the margins tend slowly to zero and windows tend slowly to $(0,\infty)$. This can be specified without a rate assumption: use windows $[1/k,k]$, margin $1/k$, and pass to each next integer $k$ only after its finite Riemann errors, feasibility bounds and the concentration errors below are smaller than the prescribed margins; the preceding compact-window estimates hold uniformly on the chosen compact transition range. The profile moments $M_1,M_2$ give relative variances $O((nh_0)^{-1})=O(n^{-1/2})$ for both random constraint sums before the slowly varying window constants. Choose the numerical diagonal slowly enough that those relative variances divided by $\tau^2$ tend to zero. Chebyshev then puts prior probability $1-o(1)$ on the actual alternative. Each draw has finite coordinate support and hence is in $\ell^2$. The prior cost tends to $U^2$, its largest coordinate cost tends to zero, and its cost on $z_i>B$ tends uniformly to zero as $B\to\infty$, by the bounded small-end and exponential large-end envelopes in [F2]. Let $\Pi$ denote this finite-support prior on parameter sequences, let $\mathcal A$ be the event that a draw satisfies both alternative constraints, and put $p=\Pi(\mathcal A)=1-o(1)$. If $p=1$, conditioning changes no mixture law. Otherwise, eventually $0<p<1$ and the unconditioned observation law decomposes as $P_\Pi=pP_{\Pi\mid\mathcal A}+(1-p)P_{\Pi\mid\mathcal A^c}$. For every measurable event $E$, this gives $|P_\Pi(E)-P_{\Pi\mid\mathcal A}(E)|=(1-p)|P_{\Pi\mid\mathcal A^c}(E)-P_{\Pi\mid\mathcal A}(E)|\le1-p$, so [F11] yields $\|P_\Pi-P_{\Pi\mid\mathcal A}\|_{\rm TV}\le1-p$. For every randomized test $\psi$ with values in $[0,1]$, the functions $N^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^N\mathbf1_{\{\psi\ge k/N\}}$ approximate $\psi$ uniformly within $1/N$; applying the event bound to each summand and letting $N\to\infty$ gives $|\mathbb E_{P_\Pi}\psi-\mathbb E_{P_{\Pi\mid\mathcal A}}\psi|\le1-p=o(1)$ uniformly over tests.

In the Gaussian branch, with the profile notation of step 1.3, for the matching upper bounds define the product-Borel score $$F(X)=\sum_{i\ge1}h_ie^{-z_i^2/2}\cosh(z_iX_i)-\sum_{i\ge1}h_i.$$ The first series is nonnegative and may be infinite; then the test rejects. Under the null its expectation is $\sum h_i<\infty$, so it is finite almost surely by [F6], and its centered partial sums converge in mean square with variance $V$. The bounded-amplitude fourth-moment calculation in step 1.2 and [F3], followed by the null variance tail bound in [F2], give $F\Rightarrow N(0,U_0^2)$. For $n$ large put $$Q_i^2=2\log(i+1)+4\log\log(i+3)+4\log\log n,\qquad \mathcal Y=\{\exists i:|X_i|>Q_i\}.$$ Step 1.2 and a countable union bound give $\mathbb P_0(\mathcal Y)\le2(\log n)^{-2}\sum_{i\ge1}[(i+1)(\log(i+3))^2]^{-1}=o(1)$. For every fixed $K$, $\max_{i\le n(\log n)^K}Q_i=\sqrt{2\log n}+o(\sqrt{\log n})$. Reject on $\{F>H_\ell\sqrt V\}\cup\mathcal Y$ for the significance problem, and on $\{F>V/2\}\cup\mathcal Y$ for total error. These are unions with a centered-cosh score, rather than an intersection or a positive-exponential uncentered score.

Now suppose $\lambda\le0$, put $e=2\beta-qs\ge0$, $n=r^{-1/\alpha}$, $m=r^{s/\alpha}$, $A_\varepsilon=m/\varepsilon$ and $D_\varepsilon=A_\varepsilon-\sqrt{2\log n}$. Every alternative has an index $i\le\lfloor n\rfloor$ with $|\eta_i|\ge m$. Indeed with $w_i=i^{qs}|\eta_i|^q$, its energy summand is $w_i i^e|\eta_i|^{2-q}$. If $i\le n$ and $|\eta_i|<m$, this multiplier is strictly below $n^em^{2-q}=r^2$. If $i>n$, the termwise budget gives $|\eta_i|\le i^{-s}$, so the multiplier is at most $i^{-2\alpha}<r^2$. If all the indicated coordinates were smaller than $m$, summing with $\sum w_i\le1$ would give energy strictly below $r^2$, a contradiction. Let $N=\lfloor n\rfloor$ and $t_N=\sqrt{2\log N}$. The finite maximum test $R=\mathbf1\{\max_{i\le N}|X_i|>t_N\}$ has size $p_0\le2N\overline\Phi(t_N)=O(1/t_N)=o(1)$ by step 1.2. Its maximal type-II error is at most $\Phi(t_N-A_\varepsilon)=\Phi(-D_\varepsilon)+o(1)$, uniformly in $A_\varepsilon$, since $t_N-\sqrt{2\log n}\to0$ and $\Phi'$ is bounded. For significance $\ell$, the randomized test $\rho+(1-\rho)R$ with $\rho=(\ell-p_0)/(1-p_0)$ is eventually valid and has size exactly $\ell$; its type-II error is at most $(1-\ell)\Phi(-D_\varepsilon)+o(1)$. The unrandomized maximum gives the total-error upper bound.

In the Gaussian branch, with the profile notation of step 1.3, under the null put $A_i=g_i\xi_{z_i}(G_i)$ for the finite prior in step 2.2. They are centered and independent, and $\sum\mathbb E A_i^2\to U_0^2$ along any subsequence with $U\to U_0\in(0,\infty)$. On $z_i\le B$, step 1.2 and the vanishing maximum coordinate variance give $\sum\mathbb E A_i^4\to0$. The omitted linear sum has variance tending uniformly to zero as $B\to\infty$; the omitted quadratic sum has expectation tending to zero. Apply [F3] to the finite bounded-amplitude arrays and then let $B\to\infty$, using Chebyshev for the linear tail. The same fourth-moment bound gives concentration of their quadratic sums. Thus $$\sum A_i\ \Rightarrow\ N(0,U_0^2),\qquad \sum A_i^2\to U_0^2,\qquad \max_i|A_i|\to0$$ in probability for the last two limits. Each factor $1+A_i=1-g_i+g_ie^{-z_i^2/2}\cosh(z_iG_i)$ is positive. On $\max|A_i|\le\delta<1/2$, [F10] gives $|\sum\log(1+A_i)-\sum A_i+\tfrac12\sum A_i^2|\le C\delta\sum A_i^2$. Let $\delta\downarrow0$. The likelihood from step 1.1 therefore has $\log L\Rightarrow N(-U_0^2/2,U_0^2)$. The addition of terms converging in probability and the successive tail limits preserve the displayed distribution limit by squeezing distribution functions between thresholds differing by an arbitrary positive tolerance.

In the Gaussian branch, with the profile notation of step 1.3, fix $d\in(0,1)$. Alternatives with $\mathbb P_\mu(\mathcal Y^c)<d$ already have type-II error below $d$. For every other alternative, writing $p_i=\mathbb P_\mu(|X_i|>Q_i)$, finite independence gives $\prod_{i\le m}(1-p_i)\ge d$ for each $m$. Hence $\sum_i p_i\le-\log d$ and $|\mu_i|\le Q_i+C_d$, the latter because the probability of the inside interval is at most $\Phi(Q_i-|\mu_i|)$. Choose $K>(2-q)/(2L)$ and $N=\lceil n(\log n)^K\rceil$. The energy of indices $i>N$ is at most $$\varepsilon^{-q}\sup_{i>N}i^{-L}(Q_i+C_d)^{2-q}\le C_d\varepsilon^{-q}N^{-L}(\log N)^{(2-q)/2}=o(r^2\varepsilon^{-2}).$$ The envelope is eventually decreasing and $\varepsilon^{-q}n^{-L}$ is a fixed multiple of $r^2\varepsilon^{-2}$. Among $i\le N$ delete those with $|\mu_i|>c\sqrt{\log n}$, where $c=0.45\in(\sqrt2-1,1/2)$. The lower Mills bound in step 1.2 implies $p_i\ge n^{-a+o(1)}$ there, with $a=(\sqrt2-c)^2/2<1/2$, uniformly over these indices. Thus at most $n^{a+o(1)}$ are deleted. Their energy is at most $n^{2\beta+a+o(1)}=o(n^{2\beta+1/2})=o(r^2\varepsilon^{-2})$, including the polynomial logarithmic factors from $N$ and the means. Define $\mu_i^*=\mu_i$ for $i\le N$ not deleted and $\mu_i^*=0$ for every deleted index and every $i>N$. This vector has finite support, satisfies $|\mu_i^*|\le c\sqrt{\log n}$, and has no increased $q$-budget. Its energy loss is at most the sum of the already bounded tail energy and deleted-coordinate energy, so its retained energy is $(1-o(1))r^2\varepsilon^{-2}$. Its score mean $M=\mathbb E_{\mu^*}F$ is therefore at least $U^2-o(1)$ by the certificate in step 1.3 and $c_0=(c_1-c_2)/2$. Coordinatewise $|\mu_i^*|\le|\mu_i|$, and $|G+\mu|$ is stochastically increasing in $|\mu|$, since $\Phi(t-|\mu|)-\Phi(-t-|\mu|)$ decreases with $|\mu|$. Independence and the positive coefficients imply the score comparison for every finite partial sum. The full score event is the decreasing intersection of these partial-sum events after adding the fixed $\sum h_i$; [F12] passes the comparison to the full nonnegative series, giving $\mathbb P_\mu(F\le t)\le\mathbb P_{\mu^*}(F\le t)$.

In the degenerate branch, with the notation of step 2.4, for the matching degenerate lower bound first take $D_\varepsilon\to d\in\mathbb R$. Put $M=\lfloor n/(\log n)^2\rfloor$, $I=\{\lfloor n\rfloor-M+1,\ldots,\lfloor n\rfloor\}$, and mix uniformly over indices $i\in I$ and signs with $\eta_i=\pm r i^{-\beta}$, all other coordinates zero. Every point has energy $r^2$ and budget $(ri^\alpha)^q\le1$. Write $T=\sqrt{2\log M}$ and $\mu_i=r/(\varepsilon i^\beta)$; uniformly on $I$, $\mu_i=T+d+o(1)$ since $M/n=O((\log n)^{-2})$ and $T-\sqrt{2\log n}\to0$. The null likelihood from step 1.1 is $L=M^{-1}\sum_{i\in I}e^{-\mu_i^2/2}\cosh(\mu_iG_i)$. Truncate each summand to $|G_i|\le T$, obtaining $\widetilde L$. Completing the square gives its summand mean $\Phi(T-\mu_i)-\Phi(-T-\mu_i)\to c=\Phi(-d)$ and its second moment at most $\tfrac12e^{\mu_i^2}\Phi(T-2\mu_i)+\tfrac12e^{-\mu_i^2}$. The upper Mills bound and $$\mu_i^2-\tfrac12(2\mu_i-T)^2-\log M=-(\mu_i-T)^2$$ bound this second moment divided by $M$ by $O(1/T)$. Independence gives $\operatorname{Var}\widetilde L=O(1/T)\to0$, and $\mathbb P_0(L\ne\widetilde L)\le2M\overline\Phi(T)=O(1/T)\to0$. Thus $\mathbb E_0|\widetilde L-c|\to0$ and $L\to c$ in null probability. Since $L\ge\widetilde L$, every size-$\ell$ test has mixture type-II error at least $c(1-\ell)-\mathbb E|\widetilde L-c|$; every total error is at least $\mathbb E\min(1,L)\to c$. Bounded convergence in probability here follows directly by splitting at any fixed positive deviation; no likelihood uniform integrability is asserted. This proves both lower bounds for finite $d$.

In the Gaussian branch, with the profile notation of step 1.3, for any likelihood $L$, randomized test $\chi$ and $c>0$, scalar algebra gives $L(1-\chi)\ge\min(L,c)-c\chi$. The limit law in step 3.1 has no positive atoms, so $$\mathbb E_0\min(L,c)=\int_0^c\mathbb P_0(L>t)\,dt$$ converges by [F8]; the identity itself follows first for step functions and then by increasing finite subdivisions. Choose $c=\exp(-U_0^2/2+U_0H_\ell)$. Its limiting upper-tail probability is $\ell$, and completing the square gives the limiting lower bound $\Phi(H_\ell-U_0)$ for every test of size at most $\ell$. Likewise every total error is at least $\mathbb E_0\min(1,L)\to2\Phi(-U_0/2)$. Conditioning in step 2.2 costs only $o(1)$ uniformly over tests. This proves both minimax lower bounds on compact transitions without an additional Neyman--Pearson or unrestricted-choice supplier.

In the Gaussian branch, with the profile notation of step 1.3, for the residual vector set $m_i=h_i(\cosh(z_i\mu_i^*)-1)$, so $M=\sum m_i\ge0$. The exact variance formula in step 1.2 shows that the excess above $V$ is $$\sum h_i^2(e^{z_i^2}-1)\sinh^2(z_i\mu_i^*)\le\sum K_i m_i,\qquad K_i=h_i(e^{z_i^2}-1)(\cosh(z_i\mu_i^*)+1).$$ For $z_i\le\sqrt{\log n}$, the global bound $\psi(z)(e^{z^2}-1)\le C$ in [F2], its relation $x\le C(1+z^{1/\kappa})$ at large $z$, and $h_0\asymp n^{-1/2}$ give $K_i\le n^{-1/2+c+o(1)}=o(1)$. For $z_i>\sqrt{\log n}$ the other global bound in [F2] gives an absolute excess bound $$C h_0^2\sum_{z_i>\sqrt{\log n}}(i/n)^{4\beta}\exp(-z_i^2+2cz_i\sqrt{\log n})\le C h_0^2\sum_{z_i>\sqrt{\log n}}(i/n)^{4\beta}e^{-(1-2c)z_i^2}=o(1).$$ The final estimate follows from the exponential profile tail and $h_0^2n=O(1)$; its discrete tail is bounded by the integral of an eventually decreasing polynomial-times-exponential envelope plus a mesh term, as in [F2]. Thus uniformly over residual alternatives, $\operatorname{Var}_{\mu^*}F\le V+o(1)M+o(1)$. Unbounded $z_i$ have been controlled by an absolute variance bound, not a uniform bounded-amplitude assumption.

In the degenerate branch, with the notation of step 2.4, if $D_\varepsilon\to+\infty$, step 2.4 settles both errors by nonnegativity. If $D_\varepsilon\to-\infty$, fix $K>0$. The continuous strictly increasing function $r\mapsto\varepsilon^{-1}r^{s/\alpha}-\sqrt{(2/\alpha)\log(1/r)}$ ranges from $-\infty$ to a positive value on $(0,1)$, so it has a unique radius $r_{\varepsilon,K}$ at value $-K$, and this radius tends to zero. Eventually $r<r_{\varepsilon,K}$; inclusion of alternative sets and step 3.3 give lower limits at least $\Phi(K)$ for total error and $(1-\ell)\Phi(K)$ for type-II error. Let $K\to\infty$. Subsequences in the extended real line now establish the two degenerate formulas for arbitrary $D_\varepsilon$. Finally put $p=s/\alpha$ and $\Lambda=(2/s)^{\alpha/(2s)}$, so $\Lambda^p=\sqrt{2/s}$. For each fixed $c>0$, direct substitution into the displayed $r_\varepsilon^*$ gives $$D_\varepsilon(cr_\varepsilon^*)=(c^p-1)\sqrt{2\log(\varepsilon^{-1})/s}+o(1).$$ The logarithmic correction is $O(\log\log(\varepsilon^{-1})/\sqrt{\log(\varepsilon^{-1})})$, which tends to zero. Thus the stated sharp constant, zero/infinite-ratio separation limits and the assignment of $\lambda=0$ all follow, with no strict inequality imposed on $e$.

In the Gaussian branch, with the profile notation of step 1.3, if $M$ stays bounded, fix $B>0$. For $z_i\le B$, $h_iz_i^2\le C_Bh_0(i/n)^{2\beta}$ by [F2]. Writing the hyperbolic addition formula and using $|\sinh(z\mu)|\le z|\mu|e^{B|\mu|}$ gives $$\mathbb E\left|h_i\bigl(\xi_{z_i}(G_i+\mu_i^*)-\mathbb E\xi_{z_i}(G_i+\mu_i^*)\bigr)\right|^4\le C_B(h_iz_i^2)^4(1+|\mu_i^*|^4)e^{4B|\mu_i^*|}.$$ Here the fourth moments of $\cosh(zG)-\mathbb E\cosh(zG)$ and $\sinh(zG)$ are bounded respectively by $C_Bz^8$ and $C_Bz^4$, by the same Gaussian exponential integration as in step 1.2. Since $z_i\le B$ implies $i\le C_B n$, the summed fourth moments are $O_B(nh_0^4)n^{o(1)}=n^{-1+o(1)}\to0$. The variance of the omitted $z_i>B$ centered sum is at most its null variance tail plus $o(1)$, by step 4.2 and bounded $M$. Apply [F3] to the retained finite arrays and then let $B\to\infty$ to obtain $F-M\Rightarrow N(0,U_0^2)$. The assertion is uniform in the sense that every sequence of residual alternatives with bounded $M$ obeys this limit. If $M\to\infty$, step 4.2 and Chebyshev instead show $\mathbb P_{\mu^*}(F\le t)\to0$ for every bounded threshold. These conclusions and $M\ge U^2-o(1)$ prove the upper type-II limits $\Phi(H_\ell-U_0)$ and $\Phi(-U_0/2)$. To justify passage to the supremum, any contrary sequence has either a bounded-mean subsequence (then a convergent-mean subsequence) or a subsequence with $M\to\infty$; both cases give the asserted bound. Let $d\downarrow0$ for the alternatives excluded in step 3.2. Under the null step 2.3 gives the corresponding errors $\ell+o(1)$ and $\Phi(-U_0/2)+o(1)$. If the first test has size $p_\varepsilon>\ell$, multiply its indicator by $\ell/p_\varepsilon$; otherwise leave it unchanged. Its size is then at most $\ell$ and every power changes by $o(1)$. This proves the exact-level Gaussian upper bound and the total-error upper bound.

In the Gaussian branch, write $\rho=r/r_\varepsilon^*$, $p=B/D>0$ and $c=c_{\alpha,\beta,q}$. For a comparison radius $R=t r_\varepsilon^*$, let $T^\ell_{\varepsilon,t}$ be the score-and-maximum significance test in steps 2.3 and 5.1, with its exact-level scaling, and let $T^{\rm tot}_{\varepsilon,t}$ be their unscaled total-error test. The proved estimates are uniform over each fixed $t\in[1/k,k]$: otherwise a countersequence has a convergent subsequence of $t$ in that compact interval, and all the compact-transition estimates already proved apply with a positive finite limiting $U=ct^p$, contradicting the countersequence. Consequently, for every integer $k\ge2$ there is a sufficiently small noise threshold such that for all smaller $\varepsilon$ and every $t\in[1/k,k]$, the profile dimension is $n>e$, $|u_\varepsilon(t r_\varepsilon^*)-ct^p|\le1/k$, the maximal type-II error of $T^\ell_{\varepsilon,t}$ at radius $t r_\varepsilon^*$ is at most $\Phi(H_\ell-ct^p)+1/k$, and the total error of $T^{\rm tot}_{\varepsilon,t}$ there is at most $2\Phi(-ct^p/2)+1/k$. Both tests are therefore defined on this whole compact range, and the significance test has size at most $\ell$ for every such noise level. Fix $j_1=1$ and recursively let $j_k$ be the least integer $j>j_{k-1}$, $j\ge k$, for which all these uniform properties hold for every $0<\varepsilon\le2^{-j}$. These integers exist by the uniform convergence just proved. For $0<\varepsilon\le2^{-j_2}$ define $k_\varepsilon=\max\{k\ge2:\varepsilon\le2^{-j_k}\}$. This is a nonempty finite set because $j_k\ge k$; $k_\varepsilon\to\infty$ as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$. The least-integer rule and this finite maximum specify one deterministic diagonal, depending only on the fixed model, significance level and the given $\delta_\varepsilon$ family, not on the unknown truth or the observations.

For this single diagonal, define the Gaussian-regime test family for every known radius $r>0$ as follows. When $\rho<1/k_\varepsilon$, use the constant randomized significance test $\chi^\ell_{\varepsilon,r}\equiv\ell$ and the never-reject total-error test $\chi^{\rm tot}_{\varepsilon,r}\equiv0$. When $1/k_\varepsilon\le\rho\le k_\varepsilon$, use $T^\ell_{\varepsilon,\rho}$ and $T^{\rm tot}_{\varepsilon,\rho}$. When $\rho>k_\varepsilon$, use $T^\ell_{\varepsilon,k_\varepsilon}$ and $T^{\rm tot}_{\varepsilon,k_\varepsilon}$, constructed at the smaller comparison radius $k_\varepsilon r_\varepsilon^*$, never at the possibly invalid profile dimension associated with $r$. For $\varepsilon>2^{-j_2}$ set the family to the same two trivial tests; this finite-noise convention does not affect an asymptotic statement. Every test is product-Borel, each significance test has size at most $\ell$, and every formula $\log\log n$ actually evaluated has $n>e$. Write $k=k_\varepsilon$. In the middle case the upper risk bounds in step 6.1 hold with error $1/k$, and $|u_\varepsilon(r)-c\rho^p|\le1/k$, so the attained errors are bounded by the stated Gaussian profiles plus a quantity tending to zero. In the small-radius case, monotonicity of the relaxed extremal problem gives $0\le u_\varepsilon(r)\le ck^{-p}+1/k\to0$; the two trivial tests have respective errors $1-\ell$ and $1$ whenever the alternative is nonempty, and no larger errors if it is empty, matching the profile upper bounds up to a vanishing quantity. In the large-radius case, the actual alternative is a subset of the comparison-radius alternative, so both achieved errors are no larger than their comparison-radius errors, bounded by $\Phi(H_\ell-ck^p)+1/k$ and $2\Phi(-ck^p/2)+1/k$, respectively, and these tend to zero. Also $u_\varepsilon(r)\ge ck^p-1/k\to\infty$, as required for the displayed profiles. These bounds apply to all three cases with the same deterministic $k_\varepsilon$; hence they also apply to ratios oscillating between them, without selecting a test by a subsequence.

The compact-transition lower bounds in step 4.1 extend globally by monotonicity of the minimax errors and of $J_\varepsilon(r(1-\delta_\varepsilon))$. Comparing $r/r_\varepsilon^*\to0$ with each fixed small positive transition constant gives $u_\varepsilon\to0$, $\liminf\gamma_\varepsilon\ge1$ and $\liminf\beta_\varepsilon(\ell)\ge1-\ell$; the corresponding upper bounds are the trivial tests. Comparing $r/r_\varepsilon^*\to\infty$ with each fixed large transition constant gives $u_\varepsilon\to\infty$ and vanishing minimax errors. For any other sequence of positive ratios, every subsequence has a further subsequence tending to zero, a finite positive constant or infinity, so the same lower-profile conclusion applies. Together with the globally defined upper family in step 7.1 this proves both sharp Gaussian formulas and asymptotic minimax attainment for every $r_\varepsilon\to0$, including oscillating ratios. In particular the displayed $r_\varepsilon^*$ is a separation rate with both impossibility and consistency halves. In the degenerate regime, the finite maximum and exact-level randomized tests in step 2.4 already apply along every $r_\varepsilon\to0$, because $N\to\infty$ and $p_0\to0$ irrespective of the noise/radius ratio; to define them also before $N\ge2$ and $p_0<\ell$, use the constant significance test and never-reject total-error test until those inequalities hold. Their global sharp attainment follows from step 4.3 and its matching upper bounds. No unrestricted power equivalent or undefined transition threshold is used in either family.

The separation-rate definition in [F1] allows every positive radius sequence, not only vanishing ones. In either regime the displayed positive rate $r_\varepsilon^*$ tends to zero. If $r_\varepsilon/r_\varepsilon^*\to0$, then $r_\varepsilon\to0$, so the impossibility half already proved applies. For the consistency half, let $r_\varepsilon>0$ satisfy $r_\varepsilon/r_\varepsilon^*\to\infty$ and set $\bar r_\varepsilon=\min\{r_\varepsilon,\sqrt{r_\varepsilon^*}\}$. Then $0<\bar r_\varepsilon\le r_\varepsilon$, $\bar r_\varepsilon\to0$, and $\bar r_\varepsilon/r_\varepsilon^*=\min\{r_\varepsilon/r_\varepsilon^*,1/\sqrt{r_\varepsilon^*}\}\to\infty$. The Gaussian tests of step 7.1 and the degenerate tests of steps 2.4 and 8.1, evaluated at $\bar r_\varepsilon$, therefore have vanishing total error and vanishing maximal type-II error at each fixed significance level on $\Theta_q(\bar r_\varepsilon)$. The defining energy inequality gives $\Theta_q(r_\varepsilon)\subseteq\Theta_q(\bar r_\varepsilon)$, so using these same tests at the requested radius leaves their null size unchanged and cannot increase their maximal type-II error. Thus both minimax errors at $r_\varepsilon$ are bounded above by their counterparts at $\bar r_\varepsilon$ and tend to zero. If $\Theta_q(r_\varepsilon)$ is empty, both minimax errors are zero by the explicit convention in [F1]; the never-reject test also realizes zero total error in that case. This proves the rate implications for all positive radius sequences, including nonvanishing or oscillating radii, in both regimes. All cutoffs and profile parameters used in this reduction are evaluated at the vanishing comparison radius.

The Gaussian and degenerate bounds agree with their respective lower bounds, and the globally specified tests in steps 7.1 and 8.1 attain them asymptotically, including exact significance adjustment. Step 2.1 proves the qualified extremal power equivalent, step 8.1 proves the full Gaussian separation claim, and step 4.3 proves the degenerate sharp normalization. Step 9.1 supplies the separation-rate implications for all positive radius sequences. Each test is product-Borel, using a specified nonnegative countable series or finitely many coordinates and deterministic randomization. Assume Countable Choice and the minimax detection-risk definition with $q=2$. For each $\varepsilon$, suppose $\Theta_2(r_\varepsilon)$ is nonempty and has a finite-support fourth-power minimizer $\widetilde\eta_\varepsilon$ with profile $\widetilde\eta_{\varepsilon,j}^2=z_0^2\sigma_j^2(1-Aa_j^2)_+$ as in the extremal-profile lemma. Put
$$u_\varepsilon^2=\frac{1}{2\varepsilon^4}\sum_j\widetilde\eta_{\varepsilon,j}^4,\qquad w_{\varepsilon,j}=\frac{\widetilde\eta_{\varepsilon,j}^2}{\sqrt{2\sum_j\widetilde\eta_{\varepsilon,j}^4}},\qquad w_{\varepsilon,0}=\max_jw_{\varepsilon,j},$$
and define
$$T_\varepsilon=\sum_jw_{\varepsilon,j}\bigl((Y_j/\varepsilon)^2-1\bigr),\qquad \psi_{\varepsilon,H}=\mathbf1_{\{T_\varepsilon>H\}}.$$
If $u_\varepsilon\to0$, then $\gamma_\varepsilon(\Theta_2(r_\varepsilon))\to1$ and $\beta_\varepsilon(\Theta_2(r_\varepsilon),\alpha)\to1-\alpha$ for every $\alpha\in(0,1)$. If $u_\varepsilon\to\infty$, then for every fixed $c\in(0,1)$ the tests $\psi_{\varepsilon,cu_\varepsilon}$ have total error tending to zero.

For the extremal profile, define the finite sums
$$J_1=\sum_j\sigma_j^4(1-Aa_j^2)_+,\quad J_2=A\sum_ja_j^2\sigma_j^4(1-Aa_j^2)_+,\quad J_0=\sum_j\sigma_j^4(1-Aa_j^2)_+^2.$$
The active constraints imply
$$r_\varepsilon^2=A\frac{J_1}{J_2},\qquad u_\varepsilon^2=\left(\frac{r_\varepsilon}{\varepsilon}\right)^4\frac{J_0}{2J_1^2}.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For each $n$, let $G_{n,1},\ldots,G_{n,m_n}$ be independent standard normal random variables, and let $w_{n,j}\ge0$ satisfy $2\sum_{j=1}^{m_n}w_{n,j}^2=1$. If $\max_{1\le j\le m_n}w_{n,j}\to0$, then
$$T_n=\sum_{j=1}^{m_n}w_{n,j}(G_{n,j}^2-1)$$
has mean zero and variance one for every $n$ and converges in distribution to $N(0,1)$.

Assume Countable Choice. In the Gaussian sequence detection experiment, let $v\in\Theta_q(r)$ have finite support $J$ and put
$$u(v)^2=\frac{1}{2\varepsilon^4}\sum_{j\in J}v_j^4.$$
Let $\pi_v$ be the uniform probability law on the finite family of mean sequences whose $j$th coordinate is independently $+v_j$ or $-v_j$ for $j\in J$ and is zero off $J$, and let $P_{\pi_v}$ be the corresponding mixture sampling law. Then its likelihood ratio with respect to the null law is
$$L_v=\frac{dP_{\pi_v}}{dP_{\varepsilon,0}}=\prod_{j\in J}\exp\!\left(-\frac{v_j^2}{2\varepsilon^2}\right)\cosh\!\left(\frac{v_jY_j}{\varepsilon^2}\right),$$
it satisfies
$$\mathbb E_{\varepsilon,0}L_v^2=\prod_{j\in J}\cosh\!\left(\frac{v_j^2}{\varepsilon^2}\right),\qquad \mathbb E_{\varepsilon,0}(L_v-1)^2\le \exp(u(v)^2)-1,$$
and the minimax risks obey
$$\gamma_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r))\ge1-\frac12\sqrt{\exp(u(v)^2)-1},\qquad \beta_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r),\alpha)\ge1-\alpha-\frac12\sqrt{\exp(u(v)^2)-1}$$
for every $\alpha\in(0,1)$.

Let $H$ be a separable real Hilbert space, where separable means having a countable dense subset, and let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space. A real isonormal Gaussian process on $H$ is a family $Z(g)$ of real random variables with finite second moments, indexed by $g\in H$, such that $g\mapsto[Z(g)]$ is linear into $L^2(\mathbb P)$, $\mathbb E Z(g)=0$, and $\mathbb E[Z(g)Z(h)]=\langle g,h\rangle_H$. It is also required that for every finite orthonormal tuple $(e_1,\ldots,e_m)$ the variables $Z(e_1),\ldots,Z(e_m)$ are independent and each has density $\varphi(t)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-t^2/2}$. For any finite list of vectors, expressing them in an orthonormal basis of their finite-dimensional span shows that their process values have the corresponding linear-image Gaussian law. Here $L^2(\mathbb P)$ identifies square-integrable random variables that agree almost surely. When $H\ne\{0\}$, all unit-vector marginals have the same law; write $N(a,\sigma^2)$ for the law of $a+\sigma Z(e)$ for any unit vector $e\in H$ and $\sigma\ge0$.

Let $X$ be a set, let $\Theta\subseteq X$ be a nonempty parameter set, let $K:X\to H$ be a signal map, and let $\epsilon>0$. For $x\in\Theta$ and $g\in H$, define the observation functional

$$Y_x(g)=\langle Kx,g\rangle_H+\epsilon Z(g).$$

The associated statistical inverse experiment has sample space $\mathbb R^H$ with the cylinder sigma-algebra generated by the evaluation maps $y\mapsto y(g)$, and its sampling law $P_x$ is the law of the random function $g\mapsto Y_x(g)$. Each sample is indexed by test functionals on $H$; it is not asserted to be a vector in $H$ or to have a continuous path. If $H=\{0\}$, linearity forces $Z(0)=0$ and the experiment is deterministic.

Assume AC and let $G\sim N(0,\sigma^2)$ for $\sigma\ge0$. Then $\mathbb E[G^2]=\sigma^2$ and $\mathbb E[G^4]=3\sigma^4$; in particular the fourth moment is finite. For independent centered normal coordinates $G_j\sim N(0,\sigma_j^2)$, every finite linear combination of the variables $G_j^2$ has finite second moment.

Let $(X_n)$ and $(Y_n)$ be real random variables on one probability space, and let $X$ be a real random variable (possibly on another space). If $X_n\Rightarrow X$ and $Y_n\to c$ in probability for $c\in\mathbb R$, then $X_n+Y_n\Rightarrow X+c$ and $X_nY_n\Rightarrow cX$. If $c\ne0$, define $Q_n=X_n/Y_n$ on $\{Y_n\ne0\}$ and give $Q_n$ any fixed value on $\{Y_n=0\}$. Then $Q_n\Rightarrow X/c$.

For Borel probabilities $\mu_n,\mu$ on a metric space S, the following are equivalent: (i) $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$; (ii) integrals converge for all bounded uniformly continuous real tests; (iii) $\limsup_n\mu_n(F)\le\mu(F)$ for every closed F; (iv) $\liminf_n\mu_n(G)\ge\mu(G)$ for every open G; (v) $\mu_n(A)\to\mu(A)$ for every Borel A with $\mu(\partial A)=0$.

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $t>0$. Then
$$\mu(\{f\ge t\})\le\frac1t\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a decreasing sequence of measurable sets for a measure $\mu$. If $\mu(E_{n_0})<+\infty$ for some $n_0$, then

$$\mu\left(\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n\right)=\inf_{n\in\mathbb N}\mu(E_n).$$

Let $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be an increasing sequence of measurable sets for a measure $\mu$, so $E_n\subseteq E_{n+1}$. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n\right)=\sup_{n\in\mathbb N}\mu(E_n).$$

No finiteness hypothesis is required.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $u, v : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at
every point of $[a,b]$ as functions on $[a,b]$ (The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set). Suppose
$u'$ and $v'$ are integrable on $[a,b]$ (The lower and upper Darboux integrals of a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ as $\sup_P L(f,P)$ and $\inf_P U(f,P)$, Darboux integrability as their equality, and the notation $\int_a^b f$). Then $uv'$
and $u'v$ are integrable and

$$\int_a^b u\,v' \;=\; u(b)v(b) - u(a)v(a) \;-\; \int_a^b u'\,v .$$

**The integrability of $u'$ and $v'$ is a hypothesis, not a formality.** Without
it the two integrals in the display need not exist at all, and the identity is
then not false but ill-formed; that is
the false statement that deletes it on the companion
page. The hypothesis is automatic when $u$ and $v$ are continuously
differentiable, since a continuous function on $[a,b]$ is integrable
(A continuous function on $[a,b]$ is Riemann integrable, by Heine-Cantor and Riemann's criterion).

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ and every real $a>0$,
$$\frac{x^m}{\exp(ax)}\longrightarrow0\qquad(x\to+\infty).$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Under an alternative $\eta$, write $\mu_j=\eta_j/\varepsilon$ and let $G_j=\xi_j$ denote the independent standard-normal noise coordinates, so $Y_j/\varepsilon=\mu_j+G_j$. Then $$T_\varepsilon-m_\eta=\sum_jw_{\varepsilon,j}(G_j^2-1)+2\sum_jw_{\varepsilon,j}\mu_jG_j.$$ The first sum converges to $N(0,1)$ by [F2]. The second has mean zero and variance $4\sum_jw_{\varepsilon,j}^2\mu_j^2\le4w_{\varepsilon,0}m_\eta$. Thus for any sequence of alternatives with bounded $m_\eta$, the second sum tends to zero in probability by [F7], and [F5] gives $T_\varepsilon-m_\eta\Rightarrow N(0,1)$.

Put $\delta_j=\widetilde\eta_{\varepsilon,j}^2/\varepsilon^2=2u_\varepsilon w_{\varepsilon,j}$. Since $u_\varepsilon$ is bounded and $w_{\varepsilon,0}\to0$, $\max_j\delta_j\to0$ and $\sum_j\delta_j^2=2u_\varepsilon^2=O(1)$. For $\phi(x)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2}$, direct differentiation gives $\phi'(x)=-x\phi(x)$. For each $R>0$ and $k=3,4$, [F9] applied on $[-R,R]$ to $u(x)=x^{2k-1}$ and $v(x)=\phi(x)$ gives $$\int_{-R}^R x^{2k}\phi(x)\,dx=[-x^{2k-1}\phi(x)]_{-R}^R+(2k-1)\int_{-R}^R x^{2k-2}\phi(x)\,dx.$$ The boundary term tends to zero by [F10], and [F11] passes the nonnegative truncated integrals to the full real line. Starting from $\mathbb EG^4=3$ in [F4], the recurrence gives $\mathbb EG^6=5\cdot3=15$ and $\mathbb EG^8=7\cdot15=105$. Taylor's theorem applied to $f(x)=\log\cosh x$ gives $|f(x)-x^2/2+x^4/12|\le C|x|^6$ for all real $x$: on $[-1,1]$ use the bounded sixth derivative, and outside that interval use $|\log\cosh x|\le|x|$. Therefore the summed Taylor remainder in $\log L_\varepsilon$ has expected absolute value at most $C\sum_j\delta_j^3\mathbb E|G|^6\le C(\max_j\delta_j)\sum_j\delta_j^2\to0$.

Put $F_\varepsilon(t)=\mathbb P_0(T_\varepsilon\le t)$ and $p=1-\alpha$. Since $T_\varepsilon$ is real-valued, the events $\{T_\varepsilon\le n\}$ increase to the whole space and $\{T_\varepsilon\le-n\}$ decrease to the empty set; [F8] shows that $F_\varepsilon(n)\to1$ and $F_\varepsilon(-n)\to0$. Thus $S=\{t:F_\varepsilon(t)\ge p\}$ is nonempty and bounded below, so $c_{\varepsilon,\alpha}=\inf S$ is finite. For every $x>c_{\varepsilon,\alpha}$, the definition of the infimum gives some $s\in S$ with $s<x$, and monotonicity gives $F_\varepsilon(x)\ge F_\varepsilon(s)\ge p$. Hence $F_\varepsilon(c_{\varepsilon,\alpha}+1/n)\ge p$ for every positive integer $n$. The events $\{T_\varepsilon\le c_{\varepsilon,\alpha}+1/n\}$ decrease to $\{T_\varepsilon\le c_{\varepsilon,\alpha}\}$, so [F8] gives $F_\varepsilon(c_{\varepsilon,\alpha})\ge p$ and therefore $\mathbb P_0(T_\varepsilon>c_{\varepsilon,\alpha})\le\alpha$. By [F2] and [F6], $c_{\varepsilon,\alpha}\to H_\alpha$, since the limiting normal distribution is continuous and strictly increasing. To bound maximal type-II error, consider any sequence $\eta_\varepsilon\in\Theta_2(r_\varepsilon)$. If its means $m_{\eta_\varepsilon}$ are unbounded, pass to a subsequence on which they tend to infinity; the variance bound in [F1] and [F7] show $\mathbb P_{\eta_\varepsilon}(T_\varepsilon\le c_{\varepsilon,\alpha})\to0$. If they are bounded, pass to a subsequence on which $m_{\eta_\varepsilon}\to m\ge u_*$ and $u_\varepsilon\to u_*$, where $u_*>0$. Step 1.1 gives type-II limit $\Phi(H_\alpha-m)\le\Phi(H_\alpha-u_*)$. A subsequence contradiction therefore proves the uniform upper bound $\beta_\varepsilon(\Theta_2(r_\varepsilon),\psi_{\varepsilon,c_{\varepsilon,\alpha}})\le\Phi(H_\alpha-u_\varepsilon)+o(1)$.

The quartic term $\sum_j\delta_j^2G_j^4$ has mean $3\sum_j\delta_j^2=6u_\varepsilon^2$ and variance $96\sum_j\delta_j^4\le96(\max_j\delta_j)^2\sum_j\delta_j^2\to0$. Substituting the expansion from step 1.2 into [F3] gives $$\log L_\varepsilon=u_\varepsilon T_\varepsilon-u_\varepsilon^2/2+o_{P_0}(1).$$ Together with [F2], this implies that under $P_0$ the likelihood ratio converges along any subsequence with $u_\varepsilon\to u_*>0$ to $\exp(-u_*^2/2+u_*G)$ for $G\sim N(0,1)$.

For any level-$\alpha$ test $\psi$, set $a_\varepsilon=\exp(u_\varepsilon c_{\varepsilon,\alpha}-u_\varepsilon^2/2)$. Pointwise, $L_\varepsilon(1-\psi)\ge\min(L_\varepsilon,a_\varepsilon)-a_\varepsilon\psi$. Hence the mixture-average type-II error is at least $\mathbb E_0\min(L_\varepsilon,a_\varepsilon)-a_\varepsilon\alpha$. Along a subsequence with $u_\varepsilon\to u_*>0$, step 2.1 gives $c_{\varepsilon,\alpha}\to H_\alpha$, and step 2.2 and [F6] yield the limit $\Phi(H_\alpha-u_*)$. Since maximal type-II error dominates the mixture average, this proves the matching lower bound for $\beta_\varepsilon(\Theta_2(r_\varepsilon),\alpha)$.

For every test $\psi$, $\psi+L_\varepsilon(1-\psi)\ge\min(1,L_\varepsilon)$ pointwise. Thus its total error against the null and mixture is at least $\mathbb E_0\min(1,L_\varepsilon)$. By step 2.2 and [F6] this expectation tends along $u_\varepsilon\to u_*$ to $2\Phi(-u_*/2)$, giving the matching minimax lower bound for $\gamma_\varepsilon$. The weighted test at threshold $u_\varepsilon/2$ has type-I limit $\Phi(-u_*/2)$ and maximal type-II upper limit $\Phi(-u_*/2)$ by the same bounded-mean/unbounded-mean split as step 2.1. Continuity in $u_*$ and compactness of the allowed range of $u_\varepsilon$ turn the subsequential bounds into the stated $o(1)$ formulas.

For $\varepsilon>0$, put $\eta_j=\theta_j/\sigma_j$ and observe $Y_j=Z_j/\sigma_j=\eta_j+\varepsilon\xi_j$, where $Z$ is the normalized observation in the Gaussian sequence inverse model and the $\xi_j$ are independent standard normal random variables. For $0<q\le2$ and $r>0$, define
$$\Theta_q(r)=\left\{\eta\in\mathbb R^{\mathbb N_{>0}}:(\sigma_j\eta_j)_{j\ge1}\in\ell^2,\ \sum_{j=1}^{\infty}|a_j\sigma_j\eta_j|^q\le1,\ \sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\sigma_j^2\eta_j^2\ge r^2\right\}.$$
Test $H_0:\eta=0$ against $H_1:\eta\in\Theta_q(r)$ by a product-Borel measurable randomized test $\psi:\mathbb R^{\mathbb N_{>0}}\to[0,1]$, where $\psi(y)$ is the rejection probability. Its type-I error and maximal type-II error are
$$\alpha_\varepsilon(\psi)=\mathbb E_{\varepsilon,0}\psi,\qquad \beta_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r),\psi)=\sup_{\eta\in\Theta_q(r)}\mathbb E_{\varepsilon,\eta}(1-\psi).$$
When $\Theta_q(r)=\varnothing$, define $\beta_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r),\psi)=\beta_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r),\alpha)=\gamma_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r))=0$, the convention that no type-II error occurs when no alternative is possible. For $\alpha\in(0,1)$ define
$$\beta_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r),\alpha)=\inf_{\psi:\,\alpha_\varepsilon(\psi)\le\alpha}\beta_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r),\psi),\qquad \gamma_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r))=\inf_\psi\{\alpha_\varepsilon(\psi)+\beta_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r),\psi)\}.$$

common probability space, and let $g_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be Borel

For each $\varepsilon$, suppose $\Theta_2(r_\varepsilon)$ is nonempty and has a finite-support fourth-power minimizer $\widetilde\eta_\varepsilon$ with profile $\widetilde\eta_{\varepsilon,j}^2=z_0^2\sigma_j^2(1-Aa_j^2)_+$ as in the extremal-profile lemma. Put
$$u_\varepsilon^2=\frac{1}{2\varepsilon^4}\sum_j\widetilde\eta_{\varepsilon,j}^4,\qquad w_{\varepsilon,j}=\frac{\widetilde\eta_{\varepsilon,j}^2}{\sqrt{2\sum_j\widetilde\eta_{\varepsilon,j}^4}},\qquad w_{\varepsilon,0}=\max_jw_{\varepsilon,j},$$
and define
$$T_\varepsilon=\sum_jw_{\varepsilon,j}\bigl((Y_j/\varepsilon)^2-1\bigr),\qquad \psi_{\varepsilon,H}=\mathbf1_{\{T_\varepsilon>H\}}.$$
If $u_\varepsilon\to0$, then $\gamma_\varepsilon(\Theta_2(r_\varepsilon))\to1$ and $\beta_\varepsilon(\Theta_2(r_\varepsilon),\alpha)\to1-\alpha$ for every $\alpha\in(0,1)$. If $u_\varepsilon\to\infty$, then for every fixed $c\in(0,1)$ the tests $\psi_{\varepsilon,cu_\varepsilon}$ have total error tending to zero.

For the extremal profile, define the finite sums
$$J_1=\sum_j\sigma_j^4(1-Aa_j^2)_+,\quad J_2=A\sum_ja_j^2\sigma_j^4(1-Aa_j^2)_+,\quad J_0=\sum_j\sigma_j^4(1-Aa_j^2)_+^2.$$
The active constraints imply
$$r_\varepsilon^2=A\frac{J_1}{J_2},\qquad u_\varepsilon^2=\left(\frac{r_\varepsilon}{\varepsilon}\right)^4\frac{J_0}{2J_1^2}.$$

Assume the minimax detection-risk definition with $q=2$, and let $a_j$ and $\sigma_j$ be positive nondecreasing sequences tending to infinity. There is a constant $r_0>0$ such that for every $r\in(0,r_0)$ there exist $A,z_0>0$ with finite nonempty $S=\{j:Aa_j^2<1\}$ for which
$$\widetilde\eta_j^2=z_0^2\sigma_j^2(1-Aa_j^2)_+$$
satisfies
$$\sum_{j\ge1}\sigma_j^2\widetilde\eta_j^2=r^2,\qquad \sum_{j\ge1}a_j^2\sigma_j^2\widetilde\eta_j^2=1.$$

Assume the minimax detection-risk definition, $q=2$, and positive nondecreasing sequences $a_j$ and $\sigma_j$ with $a_j\to\infty$. Let $A,z_0>0$ and suppose $S=\{j:Aa_j^2<1\}$ is finite and nonempty. Define $\widetilde\eta_j^2=z_0^2\sigma_j^2(1-Aa_j^2)_+$ and assume
$$\sum_{j\ge1}\sigma_j^2\widetilde\eta_j^2=r^2,\qquad \sum_{j\ge1}a_j^2\sigma_j^2\widetilde\eta_j^2=1.$$
Then $\widetilde\eta\in\Theta_2(r)$ and minimizes $\sum_{j\ge1}\eta_j^4$ over $\Theta_2(r)$; the nonnegative minimizer is unique.

derivations.claim: Let $m$ be the largest active index, so $(m+1)^{-2\alpha}\le A<m^{-2\alpha}$, and write $\ell=m-j$. For $1\le\ell\le m/2$, the mean-value theorem applied to $x^{2\alpha}$ on $[1/2,1]$ gives $$c_\alpha\frac{\ell+1}{m}\le1-A(m-\ell)^{2\alpha}\le C_\alpha\frac{\ell+1}{m}.$$ For $\ell>m/2$, the profile factor is at most one. Summing against $\sigma_j^4=e^{4\beta m}e^{-4\beta\ell}$, the near terms are bounded by the convergent sums $\sum_{\ell\ge0}(\ell+1)e^{-4\beta\ell}$ and $\sum_{\ell\ge0}(\ell+1)^2e^{-4\beta\ell}$, and the far tail is exponentially smaller than $m^{-2}$. The $\ell=1$ term supplies matching lower bounds. Thus $$J_1\asymp J_2\asymp e^{4\beta m}/m,\qquad J_0\asymp e^{4\beta m}/m^2.$$ For $J_2$, its extra factor $Aa_j^2$ is at most one and is bounded below by a positive constant at $j=m-1$. Consequently [F1] gives $r^2\asymp A\asymp m^{-2\alpha}$ and $u_\varepsilon^2\asymp\varepsilon^{-4}r^4e^{-4\beta m}$.

The cutoff relation implies $m\asymp r^{-1/\alpha}$. For $r_\varepsilon^*=(\log\varepsilon^{-1}/\beta)^{-\alpha}$, if $r_\varepsilon/r_\varepsilon^*\to0$, then $m/(\log\varepsilon^{-1}/\beta)\to\infty$, so the expression in step 1.1 tends to zero. If the ratio tends to infinity while $r_\varepsilon\to0$, then $m=o(\log\varepsilon^{-1})$ and $\log u_\varepsilon^2=4\log\varepsilon^{-1}-4\beta m+4\log r_\varepsilon+O(1)\to\infty$, because $\log(1/r_\varepsilon)=O(\log\log\varepsilon^{-1})$. If $r_\varepsilon$ does not tend to zero, reduce to $\bar r_\varepsilon=\sqrt{r_\varepsilon r_\varepsilon^*}$. Nonempty alternatives satisfy $r_\varepsilon^2\le a_1^{-2}$ by the two q=2 constraints, so $\bar r_\varepsilon\to0$ and $\bar r_\varepsilon/r_\varepsilon^*\to\infty$. The inclusion $\Theta_2(r_\varepsilon)\subseteq\Theta_2(\bar r_\varepsilon)$ transfers consistent tests to the original class. By [F1], these limits prove the displayed rate.

derivations.claim: Let $m$ be the largest active index and put $t=Ae^{2\alpha m}\in[e^{-2\alpha},1)$. For $j=m-\ell$, the profile factor is $\rho_\ell=1-te^{-2\alpha\ell}$. For every $\ell\ge1$, $1-e^{-2\alpha}\le\rho_\ell\le1$, while $0\le\rho_0\le1$. The sums for $J_1$ and $J_0$ are geometric in $\ell$; their $\ell=1$ terms give positive lower bounds and the full geometric sums give upper bounds, so $J_1\asymp J_0\asymp e^{4\beta m}$. In $J_2$, the summands are $t e^{-(2\alpha+4\beta)\ell}\rho_\ell e^{4\beta m}$; the $\ell=1$ term is bounded below by a positive constant times $e^{4\beta m}$, and the geometric series gives the matching upper bound. For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in The exponential series converges absolutely for every real argument. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of The factorial $n!$ and the falling factorial $n^{\underline{k}}$, defined by recursion in $\mathbb{N}$, $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image (The canonical natural $\iota(n) = n \cdot 1_F$ of a field, Canonical naturals are positive and strictly increasing), and powers and series are those of Integer powers $a^m$ and Series, partial sums, convergence and the sum, divergence, and the tail series.

This is a real power series centred at $0$ (A real power series about a centre, its interval of convergence, and its radius in $[0,+\infty]$). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.
For every real $x$, the series $\sum_{n\ge0}x^n/\iota(n!)$ converges absolutely. Its power-series radius is therefore $+\infty$.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\sinh x:=\frac{\exp x-\exp(-x)}2,\qquad\cosh x:=\frac{\exp x+\exp(-x)}2,$$
$$\tanh x:=\frac{\sinh x}{\cosh x},\qquad\operatorname{sech}x:=\frac1{\cosh x}.$$
For $x\ne0$, define
$$\coth x:=\frac{\cosh x}{\sinh x},\qquad\operatorname{csch}x:=\frac1{\sinh x}.$$

The positivity of $\exp$ makes $\cosh x>0$ for every $x$. If $x\ne0$, then
$x\ne-x$, so strict increase of $\exp$ makes $\exp x\ne\exp(-x)$; hence
$\sinh x\ne0$. Thus all four quotients above are defined on exactly their
stated domains ([[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]],
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]]).

Let

$$f(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}a_n(x-c)^n$$

have radius $R$. For every $x$ with $|x-c|<R$, the function $f$ is differentiable at $x$ ([[def-derivative]]) and

$$f'(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\iota(n+1)a_{n+1}(x-c)^n.$$

The differentiated series has the same radius $R$.

For all real $x,y$,
$$\sinh(x+y)=\sinh x\cosh y+\cosh x\sinh y,\qquad\cosh(x+y)=\cosh x\cosh y+\sinh x\sinh y,$$
$$\cosh^2x-\sinh^2x=1,\qquad(\sinh x)'=\cosh x,\qquad(\cosh x)'=\sinh x.$$
Moreover $\sinh:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ is odd, strictly increasing, and onto;
$\cosh:\mathbb R\to[1,\infty)$ is even and positive, and its restriction
to $[0,\infty)$ is strictly increasing and onto $[1,\infty)$; and
$\tanh:\mathbb R\to(-1,1)$ is strictly increasing and onto. On their declared domains,
$$(\tanh x)'=\operatorname{sech}^2x,\quad(\coth x)'=-\operatorname{csch}^2x,\quad(\operatorname{sech}x)'=-\operatorname{sech}x\tanh x,\quad(\operatorname{csch}x)'=-\operatorname{csch}x\coth x.$$

For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, the function $x\mapsto x^\alpha$ is continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$, with

Let $g:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, with $a<b$, in a Dedekind-complete
ordered field. For a partition $P=(a=x_0<\cdots<x_m=b)$ put
$$U(g,P)=\sum_{i=1}^m \left(\max_{t\in[x_{i-1},x_i]}g(t)\right)(x_i-x_{i-1}),\qquad L(g,P)=\sum_{i=1}^m \left(\min_{t\in[x_{i-1},x_i]}g(t)\right)(x_i-x_{i-1}).$$
The supremum of the lower sums equals the infimum of the upper sums. Define
$\int_a^b g$ to be this common value, set $\int_a^a g=0$, and set
$\int_b^a g=-\int_a^b g$. This oriented Riemann integral is additive over
intervals. Refining a partition increases its lower sum and decreases its
upper sum, and any two partitions have a common refinement. It satisfies
$$\left|\int_a^b g(t)\,dt\right| \le |b-a|\max_{t\text{ between }a\text{ and }b}|g(t)|.$$
If $a<b$ and constants $m,M$ satisfy $m\le g(t)\le M$ on $[a,b]$, then
$m(b-a)\le\int_a^b g\le M(b-a)$; reversing the endpoints reverses these
inequalities. The integral is monotone in its integrand: if continuous
$g\le h$ on $[a,b]$, then $\int_a^b g\le\int_a^b h$.
If $g$ is continuous on an open interval $J$ and $x_0\in J$, then
$G(x)=\int_{x_0}^x g(t)\,dt$ is defined for $x\in J$ and $G'(x)=g(x)$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$ and $b_0, \dots, b_{n-1}$ be
reals, with finite sums as in Finite sums and finite products, by recursion. Then

$$\Big(\sum_{k<n} a_k b_k\Big)^{2} \;\le\; \Big(\sum_{k<n} a_k^{2}\Big)\Big(\sum_{k<n} b_k^{2}\Big),$$

and, in root form (Square roots exist: a unique $\sqrt{a} \ge 0$ with $(\sqrt{a})^2 = a$; the positives are $\{x^2 : x \neq 0\}$),

$$\Big|\sum_{k<n} a_k b_k\Big| \;\le\; \sqrt{\sum_{k<n} a_k^{2}} \; \sqrt{\sum_{k<n} b_k^{2}}.$$

Equality holds in the first display if and only if the two lists are
proportional, in the symmetric sense that there is a pair
$(\lambda, \mu) \ne (0,0)$ of reals with $\lambda a_k = \mu b_k$ for every
$k < n$.

**No root is used in the proof of the squared form.** That form is an identity
plus a sign argument in the ordered field, and the root form is only a
restatement of it through the monotonicity of squaring on the nonnegatives
(Squaring is monotone on the nonnegatives); the root enters nowhere but the last step, where

square-root symbol. This matters here, because it makes the squared
inequality independent of the existence theorem for roots.

derivations.claim: Put $w=z^2$. The hyperbolic series give $$w\sinh w-q(\cosh w-1)=\sum_{k\ge1}\frac{(2k-q)w^{2k}}{(2k)!}.$$ Every coefficient is positive because $q<2$. Replacing $q$ by $2$ makes only the first coefficient zero and leaves every later coefficient positive. The positive denominators in $a,b$ therefore prove $a(z),b(z)>0$.

For fixed $z>0$ and $v>0$, put $f(v)=(\cosh(zv)-1-a(z)v^2)/v^q$. Differentiation and the absolutely convergent series show that $$\frac{f'(v)}{v^{1-q}}=\sum_{k\ge1}\frac{(2k-q)z^{2k}v^{2k-2}}{(2k)!}-(2-q)a(z).$$ This expression is strictly increasing in $v$: its terms with $k\ge2$ have strictly positive coefficients and positive powers. It is zero at $v=z$ by the definition of $a$. Consequently $f$ decreases to $z$ and increases after $z$. Direct substitution gives $f(z)=-b(z)$, so $\cosh(zv)-1\ge a(z)v^2-b(z)v^q$. Evenness proves the assertion for negative $v$, and direct substitution proves equality at $0,z,-z$.

The quotient representation of $\phi$ in the Statement is continuous. To prove strict increase, write its numerator series before the factor $z^{2-q}$ as $P(w)=\sum_{k\ge1}p_kw^{2k}$ and its denominator as $Q(w)=\sum_{k\ge1}q_kw^{2k}$, where $p_k=(2k-2)/(2k)!$ and $q_k=(2k-q)/(2k)!$. The ratios $p_k/q_k=(2k-2)/(2k-q)$ strictly increase with $k$.
